items.content: It was a queer, sultry summer, the summer they electrocuted the Rosenbergs, and I didn't know what I was doing in New York.
items.explanation: Plath's disoriented narrator situating herself in historical time, 1963. The political event dropped into personal disorientation is a distinctly human narrative move — refusing the fiction that private life is separate from public events.

items.content: The world unfolds beneath you like a painting still wet at the edges, the sea stretching endlessly in every direction, green-blue and alive with light. Distant vessels drift across the horizon like thoughts you can almost name, while the coastline curves away in both directions, patient and ancient. The wind up here has a different quality — purposeful, clean — as though it belongs to no one and has always been moving. Standing at the railing, you understand, briefly, what it means to be small and grateful for it.

items.content: The city existed differently before the fog lifted, its edges softened into suggestions, its corners dissolving into pale grey nothing. Streetlamps floated like captured moons above the wet cobblestones, each one ringed with a trembling halo. She walked without hurrying, listening to the muffled thud of her own footsteps, the way sound thickened here, became intimate and close. Somewhere ahead, a bus shelter materialized slowly, as though the morning were still deciding what to keep.

items.content: Below, the cities burned like scattered embers, orange and gold against the absolute dark of the earth. From this height, human life arranged itself into something almost beautiful — grids of light that pulsed faintly, as though breathing, separated by long stretches of perfect nothing. She pressed her forehead against the cold oval of the window and thought how strange it was to be suspended between one life and another, with all that darkness held at bay by nothing more than glass.
